title: A New At-Home PTSD Treatment is FDA-Approved!
subtitle: It's called Modius Spero, and it stimulates cranial nerve VIII
body_html:
If I thought APA was replete with at-home treatment options, including both FL-1001 and ProlivRx2 announced, and I’d get a break from covering brand-new neuromodulation devices.

Alas, this was not to be.

Yesterday, a brand new cranial nerve is being modulated for the betterment of humanity suffering from PTSD. It’s a surprise to me!

Cranial nerves exit the skull and do important stuff. I’m kind of a cranial nerve fan, as I explain here. Some of the nerves make behaviors happen, such as CN-VII, the Facial Nerve, which controls the muscles of facial expression. Others, like the CN-VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve, carry sensory input into the brain—in this case acoustic and “head position and movement in space” information. With ProlivRx, we (at Neurolief) leveraged CN-V (the trigeminal nerve) and a non-cranial nerve (the occipital nerve, which exists brain with the rest of the spinal cord and then runs out via dorsal rami and up the back of the head to provide sensation occiput of the head). We modulate those afferent sensory nerves in just the right pattern to relieve depression (that, per our FDA-label … is intended as an adjunctive treatment for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in adults who failed to achieve satisfactory improvement from at least one previous antidepressant medication). We call this “focal eCOT-AS.” That is not what this new treatment does. It does seem like I am beating around the bush. Here is a cranial nerve picture to belabor the point.

And now, Neurovalens announces their new Vestibular Nerve Stimulator (VeNS), with the brand name of Modius Spero, with FDA-approval as a De-Novo medical device for the treatment of PTSD.

However, for your author as a reporter on this exciting development? I know maddeningly little. That is why I spent so much time on cranial nerves and a product for depression I’m working on that I know anything about. It’s not to be obtuse. It’s cause the study isn’t published yet. Here is what we do know:

  • Trial is completed: NCT05242367 — 383 adults, active vs. sham VeNS, primary completion Dec 2, 2024. Status: COMPLETED on ClinicalTrials.gov

  • No results published there on ClincalTrials.gov.

  • From the Neurovalens website: The trial included 383 adults across the country with clinical PTSD diagnoses, with participants given either the Modius Spero headset or active sham device. In this clinical study, two-thirds of participants using Modius Spero reported a clinically meaningful improvement in PTSD symptoms.

  • The label—also not yet available on the FDA website—must say this is an adjunctive approval: The device is intended for use alongside – not as a replacement for – a clinician-directed treatment plan.

  • And they have two other products in the market already: Modius Sleep (indicated for chronic insomnia) and Modius Calm (indicated for Generalized Anxiety Disorder), are currently available exclusively to US Veterans through the Department of Veterans Affairs.

But the trial isn’t published yet, and the press release worked—I am writing about it after all!—but if you work at the company and want to talk to me, my DMs are open!

The device does have a clinical trial in depression—or a similar device at least. Again, if you work at the company (or on the trial) and want to shoot me the full text—I’ll do my journalist thing and write about it.

The FDA thinks it works. I have a lot of respect for FDA officers, especially at CDRH (that is the center for devices and radiologic health, the “device” side of the house). I will thus think it works in PTSD. However, for my personal astute take, you will all have to wait.

At Radial, until we hear more, we will impatiently wait, excited to see how this can be offered to patients outside the VA system, and what the data say!
